title: Everything is text: small tools and pipes
summary: Unix tools read text and write text, so small tools that each do one job can be chained to answer questions no single tool answers.

scheme: which address hits the server most?
text: Your web server is slow and you want to know which IP address sends the most requests. No single command was made for that question.
But four small commands, one after the other, do: one takes the address out of each line, one puts equal lines together, one counts them, one sorts the counts.
- Each tool does one small job, and does it well.
- You build the answer by chaining them.

scheme: lines of text, all of them
text: Why can they be chained? Because on Unix almost everything is text: logs, configuration files, and what commands print.
- Text is the common language: a tool that reads lines can read the output of almost any other tool.
- A format only one program understands can't be read this way: you need that program.
The pipe | joins two commands: what the first one prints (its standard output) becomes what the second one reads (its standard input).
- The tools don't need to know each other: they just read and write lines.
- Error messages don't go through the pipe: they still show on your screen, unless you send them into it with 2>&1.

scheme: the comma inside the quotes is not a
separator, but cut doesn't know quotes
JSON, CSV with quotes ─▶ a tool that reads
text: Text has a weak side: it's loose. A tool that cuts on commas breaks the day a field contains a comma.
- For simple lines (logs, lists), small tools and pipes are fast and enough.
- cut -d' ' counts every single space: columns lined up with several spaces, like ps output, give empty fields; awk '{print $1}' splits on runs of spaces.
- For data with a real structure, use a tool that reads the format: jq for JSON, Python for CSV.
